citation: Adam Brown, Sarah D'Angelo, Ambar Murillo, Ciera Jaspan, Collin Green (all Google). 'Identifying the Factors that Influence Trust in AI Code Completion'. Proceedings of the 1st ACM International Conference on AI-Powered Software (AIware '24), Porto de Galinhas, Brazil, July 15-16, 2024, 9 pages. https://doi.org/10.1145/3664646.3664757 ; PDF https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-research2023-media/pubtools/7831.pdf
source_tier: Peer-reviewed conference paper, company research (Google Engineering Productivity Research)
access_status: Fully read (full PDF text extracted and read)
sponsor_and_incentive: Written by Google employees about Google's internal code completion tool; no external funder stated. Mild incentive to show that tool design choices raise acceptance and trust.

date_and_recency: Received 2024-04-05, accepted 2024-05-04, presented July 2024. Log data window not stated; developer features use 90-day (language usage) and 30-day (codebase familiarity) lookbacks before each suggestion. Pre-dates agentic coding tools; covers multi-line completions only.
key_claims: Three groups of factors influence acceptance of AI completions: (1) suggestion characteristics (model quality score, length, position in line and file), (2) developer characteristics (language expertise, familiarity with the tool, tenure), (3) development context (test file, change size, bug type). Model quality score was one of the strongest predictors of acceptance. Language readability (expertise) was the strongest positive predictor. Test files and short/long suggestions lowered acceptance. Familiarity with the tool had small effects, smaller than interviewees described. Codebase familiarity and issue priority did not predict acceptance. Authors recommend personalisation and developer controls, and showing model confidence in the IDE. Authors say appropriate trust, not maximal trust, is the goal.
headline_figures: Model score (z-scored): OR 1.231 per SD [1.225, 1.236]. Readability in suggestion language: OR 1.305 [1.262, 1.349]. Test file: OR 0.792 [0.784, 0.800]. Suggestion length bottom and top third vs middle: OR 0.784 and 0.785. Line position bottom third: OR 0.859; top third: OR 0.938. Character position in line: OR 0.991 per character. Primary language usage (>25% LOC, 90 days) vs working usage: OR 1.041; no usage: OR 0.909; some usage: OR 0.959. Change size XS: OR 0.870; L: OR 1.146; XL: OR 1.148 (ref Size S). Bug fix: OR 0.959; internal cleanup: OR 0.845. Tenure <6 months: OR 1.073; 3-5 years: OR 0.956 (ref 1-3 years). Overall suggestions seen: OR 1.0002 per suggestion (about 2% per SD of 101). Suggestions seen per day: OR 0.994. Not significant: bug priority (mostly), job level (mostly), codebase and file familiarity. Pseudo R2 0.182, N = 1,000,098. 85% of suggestions linked to an issue. Model reached about 50% acceptance even at the highest predicted-acceptance confidence.
sample_unit_and_population: Interviews: 12 Google software developers, 60-minute semi-structured, thematic analysis. Logs: 1M multi-line code completion suggestions seen by 59k Google developers, each tied to an eventual code change. Enterprise (Google internal tool and codebase), not open source. Mixed-effects logistic regression with developer random intercept and temporal spline.
observed_vs_stated: Both. Interviews are self-reported beliefs. Log analysis is observed behaviour (accept or not). The behavioural measure is acceptance as a proxy for trust, not trust itself and not correctness.
what_makes_trust_justified: The paper does not test what makes trust justified. It measures what predicts acceptance. Interviewees said they trust high-quality, accurate suggestions and are limited by their own ability to evaluate output. The authors argue for 'appropriate' trust and propose surfacing model confidence or predicted accuracy, personalisation and user controls over when suggestions appear.
what_it_costs: Interviewees said longer suggestions carry more risk because they take a long time to review. The paper does not measure review time or cost of verification.
failure_mode_class: Over-reliance and miscalibrated trust (the paper cites prior work on less secure code with AI assistants). It does not measure wrong code or incidents.
control_that_would_have_prevented: Not an incident study. Not applicable.
limitations_stated: Google-only setting, may not generalise (e.g. students). Feature set limited by the preliminary study and logs coverage. Acceptance as trust may be incomplete: accepted code may be edited or deleted, and persistence was not examined. 'Strictly correlational in nature.' Only multi-line completions studied. Priority may not capture criticality.
counter_evidence: Interview claims that familiarity and task criticality drive trust were only weakly replicated or not at all in the logs. Seeing more suggestions in a day was associated with lower acceptance. Newer employees accepted more and 3-5 year employees fewer, which cuts against a simple expertise-increases-acceptance story. Even at very high model confidence only about 50% were accepted, so acceptance is not just model score.
verification_status: All figures and quotes above checked directly against the opened full PDF text. The note's question 'whether they track correctness' is not answered by the paper: 'quality' is the model's own predicted log-probability of acceptance, and correctness was never measured. [uncertain] only in that the exact data collection dates are not given.
usable_claim: In a log study of 1M multi-line completions from 59k Google developers, acceptance (used as a proxy for trust) rose with the model's own quality score, with developer language expertise and with change size, and fell for suggestions in test files and for very short or long suggestions. The study did not measure whether accepted code was correct, and its authors call the results correlational. Interviewees said they trust accurate suggestions, but the logs only show acceptance tracks the model's confidence score.
do_not_use: Do not say acceptance tracks correctness, or that trust here was shown to be warranted. Do not call model score 'quality' or 'accuracy' without saying it is predicted acceptance probability. Do not generalise to agents or non-Google settings. Do not claim expertise causes better judgement: expertise raised acceptance.
overlap_with_existing_essays: Unknown. [uncertain] Not checked against The Verification Gap or Checking Isn't Catching essays in this task.
